title: Flesh-Eating Maggots Are Back in Texas — and They're After Cows!
summary: Have you ever had a cut that got infected? Imagine a tiny fly that lays eggs in that cut — and the eggs hatch into maggots that eat your skin. That's what the New World screwworm fly does. And for the first time in almost 60 years, it's been found in the United States. The fly was discovered in a 3-week-old calf in La Pryor, Texas, about 100 miles from the Mexico border. This is a big deal because Texas has more cattle than any other state — worth $17 billion! The whole U.S. cattle industry is worth $113 billion. The screwworm fly used to be a huge problem for ranchers. From the 1930s to the 1960s, it cost them millions of dollars every year. But the U.S. got rid of it by dropping millions of sterile male flies from planes. These flies couldn't have babies, so the screwworms died out. So why is it back? Warmer weather from climate change is helping the fly spread north from Central America. It was found in Mexico in 2024 and has now crossed into Texas. Officials have set up a quarantine zone — a 12-mile circle where animals can't leave without being checked. The good news? The fly doesn't get into our food, and officials say it probably won't make beef more expensive. But ranchers are worried, because even a tiny tick bite can let the maggots in. Scientists are working hard to stop the fly before it spreads.
why_it_matters: This shows how a warmer climate can bring back old problems, and why scientists and farmers must work together to protect animals and keep our food supply safe.

background_read: The screwworm fly was once a huge problem for farmers in the Americas. In the 1950s, scientists invented a clever method: they raised male flies, used radiation to make them sterile, and dropped them from planes so they couldn't produce offspring. This wiped out the pest in the United States by 1966.
Texas (a state in the southern U.S. with more cattle than any other state) has many ranches where cows are raised for beef and milk. La Pryor is a small town near the Mexico border.
Climate change is making some areas warmer and wetter, which lets insects like the screwworm survive farther north than they used to.
Article_Structure: WHO: The New World screwworm fly and Texas ranchers who raise cattle.
WHAT: The fly came back to the U.S. for the first time in nearly 60 years, found in a calf in Texas.
WHERE: In La Pryor, Texas, about 100 miles from the border with Mexico.
WHY: Warmer weather from climate change helped the fly spread north from Central America through Mexico.

perspectives.description: Government officials acted quickly with a quarantine zone, and they know the sterile-fly trick already worked before. They are confident they can stop the pest from spreading far.
Ranchers are concerned because even a tiny tick bite on a cow could let maggots in, and the cattle industry is worth billions of dollars. They fear losing animals and money.
Climate scientists point to this as a real example of how warming temperatures allow pests to move into new regions, and they warn that other tropical diseases might follow.
